10.1038/s42256-025-01049-z.title: Human-like object concept representations emerge naturally in multimodal large language models
10.1038/s42256-025-01049-z.notes: The authors compare language and multimodal models with human behavioural judgments and fMRI measurements. About 4.7 million model choices among object triplets yield a 66-dimensional representation of 1,854 objects. Its interpretable categories resemble human conceptual organization and correspond to activity across visual brain areas. The article reports similarities, not identical representations or proof of shared cognitive mechanisms. The publisher identifies this as a research Article, first published on 9 June 2025. Its data statement links the human THINGS judgments, model judgments and NSD fMRI data.

10.1038/s41562-025-02297-0.title: Active use of latent tree-structured sentence representation in humans and large language models
10.1038/s41562-025-02297-0.notes: The study tested 372 human participants with Chinese, English or bilingual backgrounds and compared their responses with language models including ChatGPT. After one example, each group inferred which words to remove from a new sentence. Their choices tended to respect language-specific grammatical constituents. Word deletion patterns allowed the researchers to infer hierarchical phrase trees. Simpler explanations based only on individual words and their positions did not account for the observations. These behavioural similarities support shared structural patterns but do not establish identical cognitive mechanisms. The publisher labels this a research Article, published on 10 September 2025.

10.1038/s41467-025-56793-y.title: A neuronal code for object representation and memory in the human amygdala and hippocampus
10.1038/s41467-025-56793-y.notes: The authors use deep neural networks, ResNet and AlexNet, to extract high-level visual features from object images and compare that feature space with human neural recordings and memory performance. Across four experiments, they analyze 3,173 neurons in the amygdala and hippocampus of neurosurgical patients, including both newly collected and existing data. Some neurons respond to regions of this feature space rather than just one category. The response regions generalize to independent images and relate to later recognition and image memorability. The methods compare dimensionality reductions and full network features to check robustness. These findings link visual representations to human memory; they do not establish that the brain implements either artificial network. The publisher labels the work a research Article, first published on 10 February 2025.

10.1057/s41599-026-08299-1.title: To what extent do GPT language models capture human sentence processing dynamics? Evidence from Korean subject honorification
10.1057/s41599-026-08299-1.notes: The study compares three Korean-capable GPT language models with existing human data from four psycholinguistic experiments covering acceptability, politeness ratings, self-paced reading and eye tracking. Model surprisal identifies clear honorific agreement violations, but does not reliably explain context-dependent human judgments, optional honorific marking or delayed reading effects. Associations between model estimates and human performance are weak and vary across conditions. The findings concern these models and Korean subject honorification, rather than proving a general inability of all language models to represent human language processing.

10.1038/s41562-026-02611-4.title: Simulated responses from large language models are weak proxies for human economic preferences across 74 countries
10.1038/s41562-026-02611-4.notes: The authors compare simulated responses from large language models with existing Global Preference Survey data from 67,201 matched human respondents in 74 countries. They evaluate six economic preferences across 20 model and prompting configurations. Individual-level alignment is positive but weak. Models reproduce some demographic associations more consistently than cultural differences, and many perform worse in less economically developed or digitally connected countries. These findings limit the use of synthetic responses as substitutes for representative human surveys in cross-national inference and policy evaluation. The publisher identifies this as a research Article first published on 12 October 2026.

10.1038/s41467-024-55158-1.title: Deep neural networks and humans both benefit from compositional language structure
10.1038/s41467-024-55158-1.notes: The authors compare GPT-3.5 and recurrent neural networks with existing experimental data from 100 adult human participants learning ten artificial languages. These languages vary in compositional structure. The models are evaluated on memorization and generalization tasks tied to the human experiments. More structured input promotes systematic generalization and outputs more similar to those produced by human learners. GPT-3.5 uses in-context learning, while the recurrent networks are trained from scratch. The behavioral similarities in these artificial language tasks do not establish identical cognitive mechanisms. The publisher labels the work a research Article first published on 30 December 2024.

10.1038/s41598-025-14961-6.title: Correspondence of high dimensional emotion structures elicited from video clips between humans and multimodal LLMs
10.1038/s41598-025-14961-6.notes: The researchers compare multimodal large language models with existing emotion ratings provided by human participants in two video-viewing datasets. Models including Gemini and GPT predict human emotions evoked by video clips. The analysis compares both fixed video correspondences and unsupervised alignment of relationships among emotional responses. Broad emotional categories align more successfully than fine-grained individual videos. This concerns models predicting human reports, not evidence that models experience emotions. The publisher identifies the study as a research Article in Scientific Reports, first published on 1 September 2025.

10.1038/s41562-025-02318-y.title: Humans and neural networks show similar patterns of transfer and interference during continual learning
10.1038/s41562-025-02318-y.notes: The researchers study human cognition by comparing participants with paired artificial neural networks trained on matching sequences of two rule-based tasks. After learning task A and then task B, both learners are retested on A. Similar task rules promote transfer but also greater interference. Individual human learning patterns resemble networks that reuse or separate representations. Human experiments include independent discovery and replication samples. The observed behavioral similarities do not establish identical neural mechanisms. The publisher identifies this as a research Article first published on 30 October 2025.

10.1038/s41586-025-09142-4.title: Discovering cognitive strategies with tiny recurrent neural networks
10.1038/s41586-025-09142-4.notes: The study fits recurrent neural networks to observed human data and animal choices in reward-learning tasks to identify cognitive strategies. Human participants performed three tasks, with 150–200 trials each; knowledge distillation pooled information across participants. Small networks predicted choices better than classical cognitive models of equal dimensionality. The best human-task fits used 5–20 units, although 2–4-unit networks also beat equally dimensional classical models. Dynamical-systems analysis exposes interpretable decision strategies. These behavioral fits do not establish identical biological brain mechanisms. Nature published this research Article on 2 July 2025.

10.1038/s44488-026-00018-8.title: Large language models outperform humans at estimating society’s everyday norms
10.1038/s44488-026-00018-8.notes: Six large language models estimate population-average appropriateness judgements for 555 everyday scenarios, compared with estimates from 320 human participants and an earlier US human ratings dataset. Models outperform the average individual estimator, but share correlated errors; aggregating people improves accuracy, and combining human and model estimates works best. This measures inference of sampled US social norms, not universal morality or real-time social competence. Communications AI & Computing published this research Article on 1 September 2026.

10.1038/s44271-025-00205-w.title: AI can outperform humans in predicting correlations between personality items
10.1038/s44271-025-00205-w.notes: The researchers compare GPT-4o, Claude 3 Opus and a specialized neural network, PersonalityMap, with 254 lay participants and 272 academic experts in predicting correlations among 249 pairs of human personality questionnaire items. Empirical correlations from the SAPA Personality Inventory provide the reference. Models outperform most individual humans, but aggregated expert predictions match the specialized model and surpass the general LLMs on most measures. This tests population-level associations between questionnaire items, not the accurate assessment of every individual or general social intelligence. The publisher labels the study a research Article, published on 12 February 2025.

10.1038/s41562-024-02077-2.title: How human–AI feedback loops alter human perceptual, emotional and social judgements
10.1038/s41562-024-02077-2.notes: Across experiments involving 1,401 human participants, the authors examine how interactions with artificial intelligence change perceptual, emotional and social judgements. They study convolutional neural networks, controlled algorithmic feedback and Stable Diffusion outputs, comparing biased, accurate and human feedback. Biased systems can amplify small human biases, which people subsequently learn; participants underestimate this influence. Accurate feedback can instead improve judgements. The findings do not imply that every AI interaction increases bias, and the long-term persistence remains unresolved. The publisher labels this a research Article, first published on 18 December 2024.

10.1038/s41598-025-16339-0.title: The role of personality traits in predicting educational use of generative AI in higher education
10.1038/s41598-025-16339-0.notes: The authors use linear regression and artificial neural networks to examine associations between Big Five personality traits and educational use of generative AI. They analyze online questionnaires from 1,016 human participants, university students in Türkiye who reported prior educational use of these tools. Neural networks model nonlinear associations and identify openness as the strongest predictor. Openness, conscientiousness and extraversion are positively associated with use, while neuroticism is negatively associated. The cross-sectional convenience sample and self-reports do not establish causal effects or improved learning. Scientific Reports identifies the study as a research Article, first published on 19 August 2025.

10.1038/s41598-026-62333-5.title: An interviewer–evaluator–judger LLM framework for text-based personality inference
10.1038/s41598-026-62333-5.notes: The study predicts human personality traits from text using large language models in an interviewer, evaluator and judger pipeline. It evaluates existing text and personality data from human participants: Essays contains 2,467 essays and myPersonality contains Facebook messages written by 251 users, with Big Five labels. The separate Big-Five Backstage benchmark contains fictional characters, not real people. Reference texts are retrieved to construct context-specific personas for evaluation. Performance generally improves over baseline and fixed-persona methods, particularly for longer essays; gains vary across datasets and models. These results do not establish reliable psychological diagnosis or general social intelligence. Scientific Reports identifies this as a peer-reviewed accepted research Article, published on 23 July 2026.

10.1177/25152459251377093.title: Language Models Accurately Infer Correlations Between Psychological Items and Scales From Text Alone
10.1177/25152459251377093.notes: The authors fine-tune a sentence-transformer language model, SurveyBot3000, to predict associations between psychological questionnaire items, scale reliabilities and scale correlations from item text. They evaluate predictions against data from real human participants in a completed preregistered validation study using previously unseen items. Of 470 recruited participants, the main analysis retains 387 under revised exclusion criteria; robustness checks compare alternative criteria. Item-correlation predictions correlate 0.59 with empirical estimates after accounting for sampling error. Scale-level results are stronger but vary across domains. Synthetic estimates cannot replace empirical validation. The publisher labels this as a research article, first published online on 17 December 2025.

10.1038/s41598-026-66277-8.title: Persona-prompted LLM agents achieve modest but genuine prediction of human social media reactions
10.1038/s41598-026-66277-8.notes: The authors compare persona-prompted large language models with self-reported hypothetical reactions recorded from 1,511 human participants in Serbia. Across 27 models, the experiments test predictions of social media responses. A second, binary like/dislike task reports a chance-corrected Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.29 for LLM agents, versus 0.36 for a traditional supervised text classifier. These results support modest prediction of human behaviour, not faithful simulation of individuals. The single-country sample and isolated-post task limit generalization to live social platforms. The publisher identifies this as a research Article first published on 3 September 2026.

10.3389/frsps.2025.1460277.title: Validating the use of large language models for psychological text classification
10.3389/frsps.2025.1460277.notes: The researchers use GPT-4o to classify psychological phenomena in naturally occurring human text: reported speech in online diaries, other-initiated repair in Reddit conversations and harm described in NHS healthcare complaints. Model predictions are compared with human judgments in 1,500 manually labelled texts per task. One third of each dataset supports prompt development and exploratory validation; the remaining two thirds are held out for confirmatory validation. The paper demonstrates a validity-based workflow for these specific coding tasks, requiring researcher oversight rather than establishing general understanding of people. The publisher labels the work Original Research, published on 21 February 2025.

10.1038/s42256-025-01041-7.title: Dimensions underlying the representational alignment of deep neural networks with humans
10.1038/s42256-025-01041-7.notes: The authors study human cognition using observed human participants’ odd-one-out judgments of object images, comparing these choices with a deep neural network, VGG-16. They infer low-dimensional representations from matching tasks and compare visual and semantic dimensions. Human judgments also label the network dimensions. Human representations emphasize semantic properties more strongly, while the network relies more on visual properties. Apparent interpretability or overall alignment therefore does not establish equivalent image-processing strategies. The publisher labels it a research Article first published on 23 June 2025.

10.3389/fnhum.2025.1633272.title: LLMs achieve adult human performance on higher-order theory of mind tasks
10.3389/fnhum.2025.1633272.notes: The authors compare five large language models with human participants on written stories requiring recursive inferences about mental states. The benchmark contains 29,259 responses from UK adults collected in April 2023, with 140 statements and up to six orders of theory of mind. GPT-4 reaches adult-level performance overall and exceeds the human reference on sixth-order inferences; Flan-PaLM approaches adult performance. The evidence concerns English third-person text tasks, without establishing interactive social understanding or shared cognitive mechanisms. The publisher labels this Original Research, first published on 2 January 2026.

10.1287/ijds.2025.0124.title: Predicting Effects, Missing Distributions: Evaluating Large Language Models as Human-Behavior Simulators in Operations Management
10.1287/ijds.2025.0124.notes: The published article compares large language models with observed human data from nine behavioural operations experiments. It checks whether models reproduce hypothesis-test outcomes and the distributions of human choices, using Wasserstein distance for the latter. Models often recover decision effects but miss the dispersion of human responses, including strong proprietary models. Chain-of-thought prompting and sampling-parameter tuning can reduce some gaps. The publisher-supplied Crossref record identifies a journal article in INFORMS Journal on Data Science, published on 20 October 2026. The authors provide an accepted manuscript with the same study and manuscript identifier IJDS-2025-0124.R1 at https://arxiv.org/html/2510.03310v2.

10.1162/tacl.a.807.title: What Do You Mean? Exploring the Alleged Theory of Mind Abilities of Large Language Models
10.1162/tacl.a.807.notes: The authors compare large language models with 360 human participants, native English speakers from the US and UK, on multiple-choice interpretations of indirect speech and verbal irony. They manipulate characters’ belief contexts and conventional language cues. In these tasks, models remain below the human baseline and often fail to change interpretations appropriately when belief contexts change. Generation-based and probability-based evaluations produce different estimates. The findings concern the tested models, prompts and English text tasks, not all possible forms of social understanding. The journal identifies a research article published in September 2026; Crossref records 22 September.

10.1038/s42256-025-01068-w.title: Machine learning modelling for multi-order human visual motion processing
10.1038/s42256-025-01068-w.notes: The authors compare a dual-pathway deep neural network with visual motion estimates measured in human participants, using existing first-order motion datasets and a new second-order motion experiment. The latter includes three men, two of whom are authors, each completing 1,120 trials. A trainable motion-energy pathway and nonlinear 3D convolutional pathway feed recurrent integration. Training with glossy and transparent moving objects improves higher-order motion sensitivity and agreement with human perception relative to diffuse-material training. Model agreement supports a computational hypothesis, not proof of identical human neural mechanisms. The publisher identifies a research Article first published on 15 July 2025.

10.1038/s41467-025-58620-w.title: Natural language processing models reveal neural dynamics of human conversation
10.1038/s41467-025-58620-w.notes: The authors compare GPT-2 language model embeddings with intracranial brain recordings from 14 human participants undergoing clinical epilepsy monitoring. Participants held unscripted conversations with an experimenter, alternating speaking and listening. Model representations correlate with distributed neural responses and distinguish partly shared production and comprehension patterns; turn transitions show time-aligned changes. BERT and other language models provide complementary analyses. These correlations do not establish identical model and brain mechanisms or general social understanding. The publisher identifies a research Article first published on 9 April 2025.

10.1038/s42256-026-01228-6.title: Adopting a human developmental visual diet yields robust and shape-based AI vision
10.1038/s42256-026-01228-6.notes: The authors model human visual development using deep neural networks trained with an approximate progression of visual acuity, colour sensitivity and contrast sensitivity from infancy to adulthood. They compare face and object recognition under blur with existing behavioural data from 20 human participants. Developmental training increases shape-based decisions and robustness, bringing recognition profiles closer to those human observations. Model ablations identify contrast-sensitivity development as particularly important. These computational experiments generate hypotheses about human vision, but do not reproduce all infant sensory experience or establish causality in humans. The publisher identifies a research Article first published on 24 April 2026.

10.1038/s42003-025-09158-6.title: Generating synthetic task-based brain fingerprints for population neuroscience using deep learning
10.1038/s42003-025-09158-6.notes: The authors use deep learning to model human brain activity and cognitive differences from observed fMRI data. DeepTaskGen predicts task-related activation maps from resting-state scans. The study uses 958 human participants from the HCP Young Adult dataset, tests transfer in 637 HCP Development participants, and generates 47 contrast maps across seven cognitive tasks for 20,792 UK Biobank participants. Synthetic maps preserve some individual differences and predict demographic, cognitive and clinical variables comparably to or better than the tested actual maps and resting-state connectomes. Predictions are synthetic estimates rather than acquired task measurements; accuracy varies across tasks and transfer populations. The publisher labels this as an original research Article first published on 14 November 2025.

10.1073/pnas.2531748123.title: AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication
10.1073/pnas.2531748123.notes: The authors test whether large language models reproduce observed human behaviour by comparing generated replies with real human responses from Twitter/X, Reddit and Bluesky. They evaluate nine open-weight models and five calibration approaches using the CHAT validation framework. The data include 275 Twitter/X users, 492 Reddit users and 59 Bluesky account clusters, with 20 held-out reply messages per user or cluster. Automated detectability, semantic similarity and interpretable language features reveal persistent differences, particularly in emotional expression. Calibration can trade greater human-likeness against fidelity to the original human response. Larger and instruction-tuned models do not consistently improve realism. These findings concern the evaluated models and platform datasets, not every form of human communication. PNAS labels the work a Research Article first published on 12 October 2026.

10.1038/s41467-024-53147-y.title: A large-scale examination of inductive biases shaping high-level visual representation in brains and machines
10.1038/s41467-024-53147-y.notes: The authors compare 224 computer vision models, including deep neural networks and Transformers, with observed human fMRI responses to study human brain visual representations. The analysis uses occipitotemporal cortex data from four human participants viewing 1,000 natural images in the Natural Scenes Dataset. Controlled comparisons examine model architecture, training objectives and visual training data. Training data differences have the largest and most consistent effects on brain predictivity; different architectures and objectives can achieve similar predictivity when other factors are controlled. Many internally different models fit the brain data similarly, so predictive alignment alone does not establish identical neural mechanisms. The publisher labels this an original research Article first published on 30 October 2024.

10.1073/pnas.2512075122.title: Using large language models to categorize strategic situations and decipher motivations behind human behaviors
10.1073/pnas.2512075122.notes: The authors use large language models to model observed human behavior in five economic games with seven role-specific scenarios. They compare model responses with recorded decisions from 68,779 human subjects across 58 countries in MobLab, mostly social-science college students. Iteratively varied natural-language prompts broaden the model response distributions and mixtures of prompts are fitted to human behavior distributions. Prompt-based representations distinguish games and population groups. The paper explicitly warns that matching behavior does not establish that the model prompts recover actual human motives; the resulting explanations remain model-based hypotheses. PNAS labels this an original Research Article first published on 28 August 2025.

10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae519.title: Choosing explanation over performance: Insights from machine learning-based prediction of human intelligence from brain connectivity
10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae519.notes: This preregistered original study uses machine learning to predict human intelligence and investigate human cognition from observed functional brain connectivity. It analyzes fMRI data from 806 healthy adult participants, divided into a 610-person main sample and a 196-person lockbox sample, with external replication in 322 adults. Nonlinear prediction models are compared across resting state and seven task conditions, different intelligence components, and selected brain connections. Predictive information is distributed and partly redundant across the brain; accuracy depends on the cognitive state and intelligence component. The results support systematic interpretation of predictive features, without establishing causal brain mechanisms. The journal published the article on 10 December 2024.

10.1073/pnas.2512514122.title: Revealing emergent human-like conceptual representations from language prediction
10.1073/pnas.2512514122.notes: This original empirical study compares large language model concept representations with observed human ratings and human fMRI data. A reverse-dictionary task extracts representations from LLaMA3-70B and other language models. Tests use published similarity judgments, odd-one-out choices, category-feature ratings, and brain responses recorded while three human participants viewed concept images. The representations predict several human judgments and neural response patterns better than standard embeddings, but odd-one-out performance remains below human agreement and visual features such as color and texture are less well captured. Predictive correspondence does not establish identical mechanisms or fully human-equivalent conceptual understanding.

10.1073/pnas.2510270122.title: Parallel trade-offs in human cognition and neural networks: The dynamic interplay between in-context and in-weight learning
10.1073/pnas.2510270122.notes: This original computational study compares transformer neural network predictions with published human category-learning and compositional-learning experiments. It also tests GPT-3.5 and Llama2 large language models on a compositional task. The models combine in-context learning through activation dynamics with in-weight learning through parameter updates. Their interaction reproduces contrasting curriculum effects observed in human participants and a trade-off between flexible generalization and retention. Successful in-context solutions reduce the error driving weight updates; disrupting attention impairs rapid generalization but can strengthen retention through additional weight learning. The study models existing human observations rather than recruiting a new human sample, and provides a computational account rather than proof of identical biological mechanisms.

10.1186/s40537-025-01313-4.title: Accuracy, precision, recall, f1-score, or MCC? empirical evidence from advanced statistics, ML, and XAI for evaluating business predictive models
10.1186/s40537-025-01313-4.notes: This original empirical study evaluates classification metrics on credit-card default and telecommunications customer-churn datasets. Five machine-learning methods are tested across decision thresholds and Gaussian input noise, with statistical comparisons and SHAP-based analyses of feature contributions. In the reported experiments, the authors find F1 relatively stable and MCC useful as a complementary measure, while accuracy and precision are sensitive to class imbalance. The evidence is limited to two business datasets and the evaluated configurations; it does not establish one universally optimal metric for all classification problems. The publisher identifies the paper as Research, first published on 9 December 2025.

10.1038/s41562-026-02590-6.title: Turing-like tests for language and vision demonstrate a narrowing gap between humans and AI
10.1038/s41562-026-02590-6.notes: This original empirical study evaluates whether large language models and vision models reproduce human behaviour. It compares responses from 636 human participants and 37 AI models across three language and three vision tasks, then measures judgments by 1,916 human judges and ten AI judges in 72,191 Turing-like trials. Human judges often struggle with offline answers, while AI classifiers discriminate better. Imitation and conventional task accuracy are weakly related. Results depend strongly on test format: interactive GPT-3.5 conversations were fully distinguishable, with different outcomes in a Llama-3 follow-up. These restricted tests do not establish general human-equivalent intelligence.

10.1073/pnas.2519394122.title: Simulating human well-being with large language models: Systematic validation and misestimation across 64,000 individuals from 64 countries
10.1073/pnas.2519394122.notes: This empirical study predicts subjective well-being using four large language models and observed survey data from 64,000 human respondents in 64 countries. Natural-language demographic and attitudinal profiles are used to predict self-reported life satisfaction. The authors compare held-out predictions with OLS and Lasso models fitted to survey responses. LLM predictions recover some broad associations but have larger errors, especially in underrepresented settings, and compress differences across countries. Synthetic prompting experiments probe semantic generalization; adding contextual information only partly corrects biases. The evidence concerns the evaluated models and survey design and does not support replacing direct human self-reports.

10.1038/s41893-025-01681-y.title: Environmental impact and net-zero pathways for sustainable artificial intelligence servers in the USA
10.1038/s41893-025-01681-y.notes: This original scenario analysis estimates the energy, water and climate consequences of expanding AI servers across the United States from 2024 to 2030. It models demand growth, hardware and operational efficiency, grid decarbonization and spatial deployment. The resulting water and carbon footprints vary substantially across assumptions. Best practices can reduce impacts, but current energy infrastructure limits their effectiveness and modeled net-zero targets depend heavily on uncertain offsets and water restoration. These are scenario-dependent projections rather than observed future emissions. Nature Sustainability published this Analysis on 10 November 2025.

10.1038/s44482-026-00049-z.title: Large language models rate human happiness higher than humans do
10.1038/s44482-026-00049-z.notes: This original study tests whether a large language model can predict human affect from observed smartphone behaviour. Researchers compared Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite predictions with weekly self-reported affect from 83 human participants over up to 17 weeks. Sensor traces were converted into text diaries, with context windows between one hour and seven days. Fine-grained emotion predictions were less accurate than using participants' previous self-reports. The model tended to infer positive overall feelings even when people reported negative ones. Longer context did not consistently improve accuracy. Results concern this model, prompting design and predominantly young Android users, not all LLMs or clinical diagnosis.

10.1038/s44271-025-00391-7.title: AI outperforms humans in establishing interpersonal closeness in emotionally engaging interactions, but only when labelled as human
10.1038/s44271-025-00391-7.notes: This empirical study measures interpersonal closeness reported by 492 human participants across two preregistered randomized experiments. Participants read pre-generated answers from either human partners or PaLM 2 fictional characters during short structured text exchanges. When partners were labelled human, AI answers elicited greater closeness in deep-talk but not small-talk conditions. Disclosing AI identity reduced closeness without eliminating it. Exploratory language analysis associated greater partner self-disclosure with closeness. These results use prepared responses, a narrow participant sample and a specific model; they do not demonstrate superior real-time conversation or durable relationships.

10.1038/s44387-026-00086-2.title: Attention, not scale, drives human-AI alignment in multimodal language prediction
10.1038/s44387-026-00086-2.notes: This original study compares five pretrained systems, including large language models, with 600 human participants in a web-based Visual-World Paradigm using 100 six-second movie clips. Researchers measured human ratings of target-word predictability and recorded gaze in visual conditions. Visual context improved model-human rating alignment across the tested architectures. Transformer attention was associated with greater alignment when visual cues were informative, and attention maps from two models corresponded with anticipatory human gaze. Parameter size did not explain alignment in these comparisons. Human relevance ratings and model next-word probabilities are not identical measures; webcam gaze accuracy, model training differences and the tested architectures limit generalization. The final published study appeared on 7 July 2026, expanding the sample beyond its earlier preprint.

10.1038/s41586-025-09771-9.title: Persuading voters using human–artificial intelligence dialogues
10.1038/s41586-025-09771-9.notes: This original empirical study randomly assigned human participants to conversations with large language models in preregistered experiments around the 2024 United States, 2025 Canadian and 2025 Polish elections. Researchers measured changes in self-reported candidate preferences and voting intentions after AI dialogues advocating one of the leading candidates. Candidate preferences shifted in the assigned direction. A separate Massachusetts ballot-measure experiment also measured changes in policy support. The models' factual claims were not always accurate. These experiments demonstrate changes in reported attitudes under study conditions, not verified changes in actual ballots or election outcomes. The article was published online in Nature on 4 December 2025.
